clinicalPearls: Most childhood HIV infection is acquired from the mother during pregnancy, around delivery, or through breastfeeding, and transmission is largely preventable with effective interventions.

Maternal antiretroviral therapy that suppresses viral load, appropriate mode of delivery, infant antiretroviral prophylaxis, and safe infant feeding practices dramatically reduce vertical transmission.

Infected infants are frequently asymptomatic at birth, so diagnosis relies on virological (nucleic acid) testing rather than antibody tests, because maternal antibodies cross the placenta and persist for months.
Untreated perinatal infection can progress rapidly in infancy, with failure to thrive, recurrent or severe infections, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and developmental regression.
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is a serious early opportunistic infection, so prophylaxis is important in at-risk and infected infants.
Early initiation of antiretroviral therapy in infected infants improves survival and outcomes and is recommended as soon as diagnosis is confirmed.
A definitive diagnosis of infection or its exclusion requires a defined schedule of repeat virological testing over the first months of life.
Comprehensive care includes immunisations adapted to immune status, growth and developmental monitoring, and support for the whole family.
reference.pathophysiology: HIV crosses to the infant transplacentally, through exposure to maternal blood and genital secretions during delivery, or via breast milk. The virus infects CD4 T lymphocytes and other immune cells, integrating into host DNA and causing progressive depletion and dysfunction of CD4 cells. In infants the immune system is immature and the initial viral burden relative to immune capacity is high, so without treatment immunodeficiency and disease progression can occur faster than in adults, predisposing to opportunistic and recurrent infections and end-organ involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Failure to thrive of other cause
Recurrent infections from other immune defects
additionalInvestigations: HIV nucleic acid (virological) testing on the recommended schedule
Screening for co-infections (tuberculosis, hepatitis B and C, syphilis)
Full blood count and growth and developmental assessment
redFlags: Failure to thrive or growth faltering
Signs of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia or other opportunistic infection
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, prompt antiretroviral therapy, and prophylaxis against opportunistic infections, children can achieve viral suppression, immune recovery, and near-normal life expectancy; untreated perinatal infection carries high morbidity and mortality in early childhood.
pitfalls: Using antibody testing rather than virological testing to diagnose infection in young infants
Interpreting a single negative early test as excluding infection without completing the testing schedule
Delaying antiretroviral therapy or Pneumocystis prophylaxis in an at-risk or infected infant
Overlooking co-infections such as tuberculosis or hepatitis
